lessons.title: Lesson 1: Mapping where your time goes
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Make a simple map of the tasks that take your time each week.
This lesson builds toward: From memory of a normal week, you will make a time map of the tasks that take your time, with at least ten tasks, minutes for each, sorted into buckets and the three biggest circled.
A strategy starts with facts about your own business. For one week, write down the tasks that take your time and roughly how long each takes: answering messages, scheduling, ordering supplies, social posts, bookkeeping, quotes, cleaning up, training staff.
Group them into buckets: customers, sales and marketing, operations (ordering, scheduling), money (invoices, bookkeeping), and people (hiring, training).
You will often find a few tasks eat most of your time. Those are where AI might help, but only if the task is right for it, which is the next lesson.
Step by step:
- For one week, note each task and the minutes it takes.
- Group tasks into five buckets.
- Total the time in each bucket.
- Circle the three biggest time-eaters.
Words to know:
- Strategy: a plan for what to do first and why.
- Time map: a list of your tasks and how much time each takes.
- Operations: the daily work of running the business, like ordering and scheduling.
Try it now: Start your time map. From memory, list at least ten weekly tasks with minutes for each, sort them into the five buckets, and circle the three biggest.
You can now map where your time goes and find your biggest time-eaters.

check.q: What does a time map list?
options: Your tasks and how long each takes
check.why: A time map shows where your weekly time goes.

check.q: Your time map shows three tasks take most of your week. What would you do with them?
options: Circle them as the places AI might help most
check.why: The biggest time-eaters are where AI might help most.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Choosing AI projects by value and risk
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Score possible AI projects and pick the two to start with.
This lesson builds toward: Given at least five AI ideas, you will score each for value and risk and choose two projects to start with, with a quick win and a bigger project, each with a one-sentence reason.
Not every time-eater is a good AI project. Score each one 1 to 5 on value (time or money saved, better service) and 1 to 5 on risk (what happens if AI gets it wrong: angry customers, lost money, legal trouble).
Start with high value and low risk. Drafting social posts and answering common questions are often good starts. Bookkeeping categories or quotes may be high value but need careful checking. Hiring decisions, legal documents and anything about health or safety are high risk: keep a person and a professional in charge.
Pick two projects. One quick win to build confidence, and one bigger project you will plan carefully.
Step by step:
- List your three biggest time-eaters plus any other ideas.
- Score value 1-5 and risk 1-5.
- Pick one quick win (high value, low risk).
- Pick one bigger project you will plan carefully.
Words to know:
- Value: how much a project saves or earns, or how much it improves service.
- Risk: how much harm a mistake could cause.
- Quick win: a small project that works fast and builds confidence.
Try it now: Score at least five AI ideas for value and risk in a small table. Choose your quick win and your bigger project, and write one sentence on why for each.
You can now choose AI projects for your business by weighing value against risk.

check.q: In value-and-risk scoring, what does risk mean?
options: Harm if AI gets it wrong
check.why: Risk is the harm that could happen if AI makes a mistake.

check.q: One idea is high value and low risk, another is high value and high risk. Which would you start with?
check.why: High value and low risk makes the best first project.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Running a 30-day pilot and measuring it
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Plan a small 30-day test with a clear before-and-after measure.
This lesson builds toward: Given your quick-win project, you will plan a 30-day pilot with a before-and-after measure, with a baseline, a clear target and a weekly log.
A pilot is a small, time-limited test. Instead of changing everything, you try AI on one task for 30 days and measure whether it helped.
First measure the "before": how long the task takes now, how many mistakes, how customers respond. Then decide the "after" target: "Answering common messages drops from 60 to 25 minutes a day, with no increase in complaints."
During the pilot, keep a short log: what worked, what went wrong, what you fixed. At the end, decide: keep, change or stop. Stopping is fine; you learned something cheaply.
Step by step:
- Pick the task and write the before numbers.
- Write the after target.
- Run the test for 30 days and keep a short log.
- At day 30: keep, change or stop.
Words to know:
- Pilot: a small, time-limited test of a new way of working.
- Baseline: the "before" numbers you compare against.
- Target: the result you hope to reach.
Try it now: Write a pilot plan for your quick win: the task, the before numbers (estimate if needed), the after target, and what you will write in your log each week.
You can now plan and measure a 30-day AI pilot for one business task.

check.q: What is a baseline in a pilot?
check.why: The baseline is where you start, so you can measure change.

check.q: At day 30 your pilot saved no time. What would you do?
options: Stop or change it; you learned cheaply
check.why: A pilot is a small test, so a failed one costs little and teaches a lot.

chapters.name: Chapter 2: Connecting tools and setting rules

lessons.title: Lesson 4: How tools connect: integrations in plain words
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Draw how your business tools pass information to each other.
This lesson builds toward: Given the tools your business uses, you will draw how your tools pass information to each other, with boxes and arrows and at least one hand step that could be automated.
An integration is a connection that lets one tool send information to another automatically. For example: a booking form adds the appointment to your calendar; a paid order adds a row to your sales sheet; a new review sends you a text.
Many tools have built-in connections listed in their settings, often called apps, integrations or connected accounts. Connector services such as Zapier, Make or Microsoft Power Automate link tools that do not connect on their own. Check each tool's official site for what it connects to and what it costs.
Draw your tools as boxes and the information as arrows: "booking app -> calendar", "POS -> sales sheet". Then mark which arrows already work, which you do by hand, and which you might automate.
Step by step:
- List the tools you use: POS, booking, email, calendar, spreadsheets, social.
- Draw each as a box.
- Draw arrows for information that moves between them.
- Mark each arrow: automatic, by hand, or could automate.
Words to know:
- Integration: a connection that lets one tool send information to another automatically.
- Connector service: a tool like Zapier, Make or Power Automate that links other tools.
- Automate: make a task happen by itself without a person doing each step.
Try it now: Draw your tool map on paper with boxes and arrows. Mark at least one arrow you do by hand today that could be automated.
You can now map how your business tools connect and spot tasks that could be automated.

check.q: What do the arrows on your tool map show?
options: The order you bought the tools
check.why: Arrows show how information passes from one tool to another.

check.q: You copy every paid order into your sales sheet by hand. What would you do?
options: Mark it on your map as a step that could be automated
check.why: Hand steps that move information are good candidates for an integration.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Keeping control: approvals, costs and data
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Decide which automated steps need your approval and check the true cost.
This lesson builds toward: Given your tool map and costs, you will mark the steps that need your approval and calculate the true cost of automation, starring every step that sends money or messages to many people, and comparing cost with hours saved.
Automation saves time, but it can also repeat a mistake a hundred times. Keep a person approving anything that sends money, sends messages to many customers, changes prices, deletes records or makes promises.
Count the full cost: subscriptions, per-use charges, setup time and the time to check the work. Compare it with the time saved from your pilot. If the numbers do not add up, stay manual for now.
Know where your data goes. Before connecting a tool, read what data it can see and keep that to the minimum. Use strong passwords and two-step sign-in on business accounts, and remove access for staff who leave.
Step by step:
- Mark every automated step that sends money, messages many people, changes prices or deletes data.
- Require your approval on those steps.
- Add up the full monthly cost.
- Check what data each connection can see.
- Turn on two-step sign-in.
Words to know:
- Approval step: a point where a person must say yes before the process continues.
- Two-step sign-in: a second check, like a code on your phone, when you log in.
- Subscription: a regular payment to keep using a tool.
Try it now: On your tool map, put a star on every step that needs your approval. Then write a cost check: monthly tool costs vs hours saved times what your hour is worth.
You can now keep control of automations with approval steps, cost checks and data limits.

check.q: Why keep approval on automations that send money or mass messages?
options: Automation can repeat a mistake many times
check.why: One error in an automation can repeat many times before you notice.

check.q: A staff member leaves your business. What would you do?
options: Leave their access in case they return
Share their password with the new hire
Remove their access to business tools
check.why: Removing access protects your business data.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Writing your AI use policy and one-page plan
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Write five simple AI rules for your business and finish your one-page AI plan.
This lesson builds toward: Given how your business uses AI, you will write a five-rule AI use policy and a one-page AI plan, with all five plan parts and rules a staff member finds clear.
An AI use policy is a short list of rules for how you and your staff use AI. It protects customers and keeps everyone consistent. Five rules are enough to start.
Example rules: (1) No customer names with contact details, card numbers, passwords or employee records go into AI tools. (2) A person checks every fact before customers see it. (3) We never write fake reviews or claims. (4) Only approved tools are used for business. (5) Money, legal, hiring and safety decisions are made by people.
Ask AI to make your rules clear and short, then put them on one page with your time map, chosen projects, pilot plan, tool map and cost check. Review the plan every three months.
Step by step:
- Write five rules in plain words.
- Ask AI to make them clear and short.
- Share them with staff and get their questions.
- Put everything on one page and set a review date.
Words to know:
- AI use policy: written rules for how a business uses AI.
- Approved tool: a tool the owner has checked and allowed for business use.
Try it now: Final task: write your five AI rules and your one-page AI plan with all five parts. Share the rules with one staff member or a trusted person and ask if anything is unclear.
You can now lead your business's use of AI with a written plan and clear rules.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Time map and two projects No time map, or projects chosen without value and risk scores. Time map plus two chosen tasks, each with a value and risk score. Each choice has a clear one-sentence reason tied to the time map. 30-day pilot No measure, or no before numbers. A pilot for the first task with a baseline and an after target. Also has a weekly log plan and a stop-or-change rule for day 30. Tool connections and approvals No tool map, or no approvals marked. A diagram or list of how tools connect, with approval steps marked. Every step that sends money or mass messages is starred. Cost check No cost check. Monthly tool costs compared with hours saved times the value of your hour. Includes per-use charges, setup and checking time. AI use policy Fewer than five rules, or rules that hand money, legal, hiring or safety decisions to AI. Five clear rules for you and your staff. Shared with a staff member or trusted person and made clearer from their feedback. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: What is an AI use policy?
options: Written rules for how your business uses AI
check.why: An AI use policy sets clear rules for you and your staff.

check.q: You wrote your five AI rules. What would you do next?
options: Share them with a staff member and ask if anything is unclear
check.why: Rules only work if the people using them understand them.
